extraction.name: Evaluating Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models
extraction.description: This work presents the first systematic study on object hallucination of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs), where models tend to generate objects inconsistent with target images in descriptions. The study evaluates several representative LVLMs, finding severe object hallucination issues. It discusses that visual instructions may influence hallucination, noting that frequently appearing or co-occurring objects in visual instructions are prone to be hallucinated. The paper also designs a polling-based query method called POPE for more stable and flexible evaluation of object hallucination.
extraction.creator: Yifan Li, Yifan Du, Kun Zhou, Jinpeng Wang, Wayne Xin Zhao, Ji-Rong Wen
extraction.citeAs: Yifan Li, Yifan Du, Kun Zhou, Jinpeng Wang, Wayne Xin Zhao, and Ji-Rong Wen. 2023. Evaluating Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models. arXiv:2305.10355.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The evaluation data for POPE is constructed as a set of triples, each consisting of an image, multiple questions, and their binary answers ('Yes' or 'No'). Questions with 'Yes' answers are built using ground-truth objects from existing annotations, while 'No' answer questions are built by sampling nonexistent objects using three strategies: Random Sampling, Popular Sampling, and Adversarial Sampling. For the MSCOCO evaluation, 500 images with more than 3 ground-truth objects were randomly selected from its validation set, and 6 questions were constructed for each image. For scalability, automatic segmentation tools like SEEM were used to annotate images from MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, and GQA datasets to build POPE based on segmentation results.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Images and annotations from MSCOCO (Lin et al., 2014), A-OKVQA (Schwenk et al., 2022), and GQA (Hudson and Manning, 2019) datasets.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The evaluation data is manipulated by constructing triples of images, questions, and binary answers. Questions are formulated using a template 'Is there a/an <object> in the image?'. The ratio between ground-truth (existent) and nonexistent objects is set to 1:1 for label balance. Nonexistent objects are sampled using three strategies: Random Sampling (randomly sampling objects not in the image), Popular Sampling (selecting top-k most frequent objects in the dataset not in the image), and Adversarial Sampling (ranking objects by co-occurrence frequency with ground-truth objects and selecting top-k frequent ones not in the image).
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For the MSCOCO evaluation, 2,000 images with annotations about contained objects and human-labeled captions were randomly sampled from its validation set. For CHAIR metric computation, only 80 objects appearing in the MSCOCO segmentation challenge were considered. For SEEM-based POPE, SEEM (Zou et al., 2023) was used to annotate images from MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, and GQA datasets to generate segmentation results, which then served as object annotations.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Object annotations for the evaluation are obtained either from existing human annotations (ground-truth objects) of datasets like MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, and GQA, or from the results of automatic segmentation tools like SEEM (Zou et al., 2023). These annotations are then used to formulate 'Yes' questions for existent objects and to guide the sampling of 'No' questions for nonexistent objects.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: SEEM (Zou et al., 2023) for automatic annotation. The platforms for original human annotations of MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, and GQA are not specified.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: A potential inconsistency is noted when combining with automatic segmentation tools: objects annotated by the tool may be inconsistent with human annotations, leading to a divergence in evaluation results. The paper also validates the consistency between POPE responses and generated captions, finding a robust correlation.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: Object hallucination in LVLMs hinders their safe use in real-world deployment, potentially leading to unexpected consequences. For instance, an autonomous driving system making wrong decisions due to incorrect environmental understanding could cause serious safety issues. The work aims to contribute to developing more reliable and human-aligned LVLMs by studying object hallucination.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The visual instruction datasets used for training LVLMs, often based on MSCOCO, exhibit an unbalanced object distribution where frequently appearing objects constitute a major part. This leads to LVLMs being prone to hallucinate objects that frequently appear or co-occur in these instruction datasets.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The study focuses solely on object hallucination, not measuring the overall performance of LVLMs. Evaluation was conducted on a subset of validation sets due to computational resource limitations, meaning results might be affected by specific data distributions. The POPE method's matching-based approach for 'Yes'/'No' answers can be inaccurate if LVLMs don't explicitly provide these words. When using automatic segmentation tools, the label set might be inconsistent with human annotations, causing evaluation divergence. Finally, the study only compared a small number of LVLMs, excluding some recent or closed-source models.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The proposed POPE method is designed for evaluating object hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs). It can be used to estimate the degree of hallucination, is stable to prompt variations, and can be extended to unannotated datasets with the help of automated segmentation tools.
